meta.purpose: The transferable decision rules that generate CISA answers across every domain. Tagging questions with the rule that decided them gives a second diagnostic axis: not 'study encryption' but 'you reach for detective controls when the stem asks what prevents'.
meta.why_here: Mapping lives in this one file rather than as tags across 292 question files. One place to review, cheap to extend, and adding a principle later touches nothing else.

fields.statement: the rule, stated so it can be applied
fields.why: why it holds - the reason is what transfers to unseen questions
fields.misapplication: the rule people substitute for it. This is what the diagnostic reports back.
fields.scope: when the rule does NOT apply. Treating a scoped rule as universal is its own trap.

principles.name: Risk assessment precedes control selection
principles.statement: Controls are chosen because a risk assessment identified the exposure. Anything that selects controls from a catalog, a peer benchmark, or last year's findings has skipped the step that makes the selection defensible.
principles.why: Controls exist to reduce risk relative to business objectives. Without an assessment, the control set reflects someone else's assumptions and effort goes where it is not needed while real exposures stay open.
principles.misapplication: Reaching for the framework, the tool, or the training as the first step. All three are plausible and all three presuppose an answer to a question nobody has asked yet.
principles.scope: Applies to selecting and prioritizing controls. It does not mean a risk assessment precedes every action - during an active incident, containment comes first.

principles.name: Prevent beats detect beats correct
principles.statement: When the stem asks what BEST addresses a weakness, the preventive control outranks the detective one, and detection outranks correction.
principles.why: A control that stops the event removes the loss entirely. Detection only shortens the exposure, and correction only limits what has already happened.
principles.misapplication: Choosing monitoring, logging, review or reporting when something could have stopped the event outright. These feel responsible and are usually the second-best answer.
principles.scope: ONLY when the stem asks what addresses or prevents a weakness. If it asks about recovery, evidence, or what to do after an event, the ranking inverts and detective or corrective controls win.

principles.name: Accountability cannot be outsourced
principles.statement: Tasks move to a provider; responsibility for the outcome does not. The organization remains answerable for its data, its compliance and its risk regardless of who performs the work.
principles.why: Regulators, customers and the board hold the organization to account, not its suppliers. That is why oversight, assurance rights and exit planning have to be designed into the arrangement.
principles.misapplication: Assuming a contract, a certification or a provider's own assurances transfer the obligation. They transfer the activity and, at most, some financial consequence.
principles.scope: About accountability specifically. Operational tasks genuinely do transfer, and expecting the customer to patch a SaaS platform is the opposite error.

principles.name: Design evidence is not operating evidence
principles.statement: Policies, approvals, charters, certifications and plans establish what should happen. Only records of the control running over a period establish that it did.
principles.why: A control can be perfectly designed and never performed. Operating effectiveness is a claim about a period of time and needs evidence covering that period.
principles.misapplication: Accepting an approved policy, a signed attestation, a certificate or a documented procedure as proof the control works. Each is real evidence - of design.
principles.scope: When the stem asks for evidence of operating effectiveness. If it asks whether a control is appropriately designed, design evidence is exactly what you want.

principles.name: Completeness beats sampling
principles.statement: The dangerous item is the one missing from your list. Reconcile the recorded population against an independent source before concluding anything about it.
principles.why: A sample drawn from an incomplete population tells you only about the part that was already known. No sample size compensates for records that were never there.
principles.misapplication: Treating a clean sample, a licence count, or a vendor console total as evidence of coverage. All three describe the managed population and are silent about what sits outside it.
principles.scope: Strongest where the risk is unmanaged or unrecorded items. Not relevant when the population is closed and known.

principles.name: Contain before eradicate before recover
principles.statement: While something is actively spreading, stop the spread first. Investigation, attribution, restoration and notification all follow.
principles.why: Every minute of active propagation enlarges the loss. Containment converts an expanding problem into a fixed one that can then be worked methodically.
principles.misapplication: Restoring from backup (reinfects and destroys evidence), hunting for who caused it (belongs to later investigation), or notifying regulators (depends on a scope assessment you cannot yet make).
principles.scope: Incident response specifically, and only while the incident is live. Preparation work belongs before, and lessons learned after.

principles.name: Never sample from a population the auditee controls
principles.statement: Test from a population whose completeness you established independently, and work from the system of record toward the approvals rather than the reverse.
principles.why: A list produced by the party under review can omit exactly the records that would reveal the problem, and nothing in the sample will show that it did.
principles.misapplication: Accepting a system-generated report because it looks authoritative, or testing forward from approved requests, which can only ever confirm that approved things happened.
principles.scope: Evidence gathering and sampling. Auditee-produced data is fine once its completeness and accuracy have been separately established.

principles.name: Address the cause, not the instance
principles.statement: A finding is resolved when the mechanism that produced it is removed. Correcting the specific exceptions found leaves the mechanism intact.
principles.why: Instance-level fixes guarantee the same finding reappears at the next audit, and the organization pays the cost repeatedly without ever buying the fix.
principles.misapplication: Accepting remediation of the sampled items, more training, or a policy reminder as the answer when the process itself produced the failure.
principles.scope: Recommendations and problem management. During an active incident a workaround that restores service is correct even though it is not a cure.

principles.name: Business impact sets priority
principles.statement: Criticality, recovery order and remediation sequence follow from consequence to the business, not from technical difficulty, cost, user count or who asked loudest.
principles.why: Only the business can quantify what an outage or a breach costs it. Priorities set inside IT track system complexity and visibility instead.
principles.misapplication: Ranking by number of users affected, by monetary value alone, by cost of the fix, or by how hard the work is.
principles.scope: Prioritization decisions. Not a rule about who performs the work.

principles.name: Nobody marks their own homework
principles.statement: Whoever performs an activity should not be the one who approves, reviews or reports on it. Whoever can grant access can use it.
principles.why: Self-review removes the independent check that makes the control meaningful, and concentrating authorization with execution lets one person complete a harmful action unaided.
principles.misapplication: Accepting review by the person's own manager within the same function, or treating logging as a substitute for separation. Detection after the fact is not segregation.
principles.scope: Applies to control design and to auditor independence alike. Compensating controls are legitimate where segregation is genuinely impractical in a small team.

principles.name: Management decides, the auditor evaluates
principles.statement: The auditor assesses, reports and escalates. Management owns the decision, accepts the risk, implements the control and answers for compliance.
principles.why: An auditor who implements or decides is auditing their own work at the next engagement, and the organization loses the independent view it created the function to get.
principles.misapplication: Having the auditor fix it, overrule management, remove a finding to keep the peace, or go straight to a regulator. All feel decisive; each destroys the role.
principles.scope: About the division of responsibility. It does not stop the auditor recommending, advising early in a project, or escalating firmly to the audit committee.

principles.name: Authorization precedes action
principles.statement: Before testing, changing, accessing or deploying, confirm that someone with the authority to permit it has done so, in writing, with scope defined.
principles.why: Without authorization the activity is indistinguishable from the attack or the unauthorized change it resembles, and there is no agreed boundary when something goes wrong.
principles.misapplication: Focusing on the competence of the people, the quality of the tools, or the technical safeguards instead of on whether permission exists.
principles.scope: Strongest for penetration testing, production changes and access provisioning. Emergency procedures legitimately defer approval, but require retrospective review.

principles.name: Untested means unknown
principles.statement: A control, plan, backup or recovery capability that has never been exercised has unknown effectiveness, whatever its design says.
principles.why: The failure surfaces at the moment of need, which is the worst possible time to discover it. Testing converts an assumption into evidence.
principles.misapplication: Accepting approval, documentation, vendor assurance or the existence of the capability as evidence it works. Also accepting a partial test as a full one.
principles.scope: Universal for controls that only run under stress: suppression systems, generators, backups, continuity plans, failover.

principles.name: A tool only sees what reaches it
principles.statement: Monitoring, scanning, filtering and prevention are bounded by what is actually fed to them. Sources not forwarding, traffic not decrypted and assets not enrolled are invisible.
principles.why: Coverage gaps produce false confidence, which is more dangerous than a known absence of control because the risk is treated as managed.
principles.misapplication: Judging a tool by its configuration, its rules or its licence count rather than by what is in scope. Also assuming alerts generated equal alerts reviewed.
principles.scope: Detection and prevention tooling. Not about tuning quality, which is a separate weakness.

principles.name: A control that acts too late has not acted
principles.statement: Detection, review and escalation must happen inside the window in which they can change the outcome. Beyond that window the control provides evidence, not protection.
principles.why: Objectives with deadlines - overnight batch, breach notification, month-end close - are not met by a control operating on a monthly cycle.
principles.misapplication: Accepting periodic review or after-the-fact reporting as adequate when the stem sets an implicit deadline.
principles.scope: Wherever the stem attaches a time constraint. A quarterly review is perfectly adequate for a risk that moves quarterly.

principles.name: Direct and independent evidence outranks representation
principles.statement: Evidence the auditor obtains or produces beats evidence supplied by the party under review, which beats what that party says about it.
principles.why: Reliability rises with the auditor's proximity to the evidence and with the independence of its source. Inquiry is the weakest form and reports intent rather than behavior.
principles.misapplication: Relying on interviews, management representations, self-reported dashboards or vendor questionnaires because they are consistent and readily available.
principles.scope: Evidence reliability. Inquiry remains valuable for building understanding and directing testing - just not for concluding.

principles.name: The verb governs, not the scenario
principles.statement: The same situation has different correct answers depending on whether the stem asks for the greatest risk, the best control, the first step, or the best evidence. Answer the question actually asked.
principles.why: Distractors are built from correct answers to the neighbouring question. An option can be entirely true, and about this scenario, and still be wrong because it answers a different verb.
principles.misapplication: Recognizing the scenario, retrieving what you know about it, and selecting the most familiar true statement rather than the one responsive to the stem.
principles.scope: Universal. This is the single most common way to lose marks on material you actually know.

principles.name: Measure the outcome, not the activity
principles.statement: Effectiveness is demonstrated by what changed, not by what was performed. Completion rates, volumes produced and records opened describe effort; a measure only counts if it moves when the thing it claims to measure moves.
principles.why: Activity metrics are easy to collect and easy to satisfy without achieving anything, so they drift toward being gamed. Outcome measures resist that because the underlying reality has to change.
principles.misapplication: Accepting completion percentages, ticket counts, findings raised, or documents published as evidence a programme works.
principles.scope: Judging effectiveness. Activity measures remain useful operationally for capacity and workload management.

principles.name: Diagnose before you prescribe
principles.statement: When something unexpected appears - an exception, a mass of alerts, widespread workarounds - establish what it means before responding to it.
principles.why: The obvious response usually treats a symptom, and acting immediately forecloses the finding. One exception may be isolated or systemic, and 4,000 hits usually means the rule is wrong rather than the control.
principles.misapplication: Escalating, blocking, extending the sample or reporting the raw count before establishing what the observation actually indicates.
principles.scope: Analysis and response design. It does not license delay during an active incident, where containment precedes diagnosis.

principles.name: Cost of correction rises with time
principles.statement: A defect, a control gap or a bad requirement costs least at the point it is introduced and most in production. Involvement early is worth more than thoroughness late.
principles.why: Everything built on top of an error has to be reworked with it. By production the cost includes business impact, emergency change and data correction.
principles.misapplication: Deferring control design, audit involvement or privacy assessment until the review stage, where the finding is real but the remedy is expensive or refused.
principles.scope: Design and delivery lifecycles. Early involvement must stay advisory, or the auditor loses independence at the later review.

principles.name: Concentration is the exposure
principles.statement: Where one person, one key, one supplier, one site or one component carries the whole capability, its loss is the organization's loss. Look for what everything silently depends on.
principles.why: Redundancy is usually partial. Duplicated servers share a switch; two data centres share a grid; a resilient team has one person who understands the legacy system.
principles.misapplication: Managing the symptom - paying the key person more, monitoring the supplier harder - instead of removing the dependency through cross-training, segmentation or a second source.
principles.scope: Availability and continuity. Concentration is sometimes a deliberate and correct trade for consistency, as with centralized IT.

principles.name: A decision nobody owns has not been made
principles.statement: Exceptions, risk acceptances, go-live calls and sign-offs must be documented, made by someone with authority to make them, and time-bounded where relevant.
principles.why: Undocumented decisions cannot be reviewed, revisited or defended, and temporary accommodations quietly become permanent unmanaged risk.
principles.misapplication: Accepting informal approval, a plan to fix it later, or the absence of objection as though a decision had been taken.
principles.scope: Governance of deviations and approvals. Not an argument for documenting every routine action.

principles.name: Protection follows the data, not the system
principles.statement: Data keeps its classification and its protection requirements everywhere it goes: copies into test environments, backups, exports, third parties, and the media carrying it out of the building. Ask where else this data exists.
principles.why: Controls are built around the production system because that is where the data was designed to live. It does not stay there. Every copy inherits the sensitivity without inheriting the controls, and the copy is where the loss usually happens.
principles.misapplication: Treating the primary system's controls as the protection and copies as an operational detail — test refreshes, backup media, decommissioned drives, analytics extracts. Also assuming the purpose limit agreed at collection stops applying once the data is inside the organisation.
principles.scope: About protection travelling with the data. Not an argument against test environments, backups or analytics — those are necessary. The point is that each copy needs the control too, not that the copy should not exist.
